grand_strategy.reading:
Brazil plays the strategy of a continental power that will not take sides. It sells soybeans and beef to China, trades with the EU, speaks for the Global South in the BRICS and wants to lead on the Amazon, while US tariffs and sanctions and Argentina's feud push it to lean on its own bloc. The 25 October runoff is the constraint that decides how long this holds, because the sovereignty line that works against Washington is also the line that the Bolsonaro camp contests. Brazil's partners are many and none is a bloc of its own, so its room is the room that the vote leaves.

Enriched 2026-10-16 (protagonist pass). Read through Luttwak, Brazil is a country whose paradoxes all come from one fact: it is strong enough to be courted by every pole and too weak in arms to be feared by any. Each coercion has found it a substitute (China for the US soybean trade, the EU and Japan through Mercosur for the US market, the forest fund for the money of the rich states), and each substitute has made a new dependency (China's beef duty, the Brussels court, Argentina's veto in the bloc). The seams are visible: Washington presses it with tariffs and a Section 301 duty while Berlin, Madrid, London and Tokyo court it as a supplier of minerals and a partner in governance; Beijing buys what it grows and taxes it when it grows too much. The neighbourhood has turned right (Argentina, Chile, Paraguay, Bolivia, now Colombia and Peru) just as Brasilia needs it most, which makes the 25 October runoff a hinge for the whole card: a Flavio Bolsonaro victory would put the sovereignty line against Washington, the BRICS posture and the Gaza line in question at once (our reading: the campaign coverage read does not set out either candidate's foreign policy), while a Lula victory keeps the card as it stands, with the neighbours cooler and the tariff in place. The runoff polls are tight and lean to Flavio (Datafolha, 6-7 October: 49% to 45%, margin 2 points).
